_comment: Знания для Jev по temp/pictures/translated_foundations.txt. Для каждого типа фундамента и фактора: сила влияния и оценка (verdict + reason) для каждого значения входа. В запрос уходят только оценки для фактических значений. verdict: favourable | acceptable | neutral | unfavourable | excluded. Глубина промерзания в диапазонах формы фронта: shallow до 0,8 м, moderate 0,8-1,5 м, deep 1,5-2,0 м, very_deep более 2,0 м.

sand: Driven piles in sand reach a high bearing capacity, provided a strong bearing layer lies 3 to 10 m below.
sandy_loam: Piles perform satisfactorily in sandy loam when embedded into dense layers.
loam: Piles perform satisfactorily in loam when embedded into dense layers.
clay: Dense clay holds piles well by friction along the shaft; soft water-saturated clay needs longer piles.
fill: Ideal case for piles: they pass through the heterogeneous fill and bear on the natural strong soil below.

low: Preferred choice: piles pass through the weak layer and transfer the load to deep strong strata.
medium: Piles are still effective, especially under large building loads.
high: The need for piles decreases: cheaper strip or slab foundations carry the load without deep embedment.
Major indication for piles: they are installed without excavation or concreting in water.
medium: Little influence on the choice; piles remain applicable.
low: Piles lose part of their advantage because strip and slab foundations are easy to build in dry soil.

shallow: A shallow strip foundation is a viable cheaper option, so piles have no special advantage.
moderate: Piles are competitive, especially in frost-susceptible soils.
deep: Strong advantage for piles: they are simply made to extend below the freezing depth.
very_deep: Practically the only reasonable solution: shallow foundations at this freezing depth are uneconomical.

1-2: Light houses use small-diameter screw piles.
3-5: Medium-diameter piles or bored piles are used.
6-10: Bored or driven reinforced concrete piles are used.
11-25: Long driven reinforced concrete piles or a combined pile-slab foundation are used.
26+: Piles are the main foundation type for such buildings; piles reach 20 to 40 m.

wood: Minimal load; small-diameter screw piles are enough.
aerated_concrete: Medium-diameter piles with a mandatory monolithic grillage, because aerated concrete performs poorly in bending.
brick: Strong piles with a reinforced concrete grillage and reduced pile spacing.
reinforced_concrete: Maximum load is carried by large-section driven or bored piles with a massive grillage.

7: Pile bearing capacity must be increased by 20 to 30 percent.
8+: One of the preferred solutions: deep support makes piles less prone to failure than shallow foundations; pile tips must rest on rock or dense soil.

sand: A slab works well on sand but is often excessive, since sand itself is a good base.
sandy_loam: A slab is effective on sandy loam with high moisture content.
loam: A slab spreads the load evenly and moves with frost-susceptible, heterogeneous loam as a single unit.
clay: A slab spreads the load evenly and moves with frost-susceptible, heterogeneous clay as a single unit.
fill: One of the best options: the slab prevents uneven settlement while the fill self-compacts; the base must be compacted.

low: Preferred: the large bearing area cuts the pressure on the soil 3 to 5 times compared with a strip.
medium: A slab is effective under large building loads.
high: A slab is excessive and economically unjustified; a strip foundation is sufficient.
Major indication for a slab: a waterproofed slab is a reliable barrier and works as a floating structure; uplift must be checked.
low: The advantage of a slab is smaller, but it is still useful on frost-susceptible soils.

shallow: Weak influence; the choice depends on other factors.
moderate: An insulated slab effectively counteracts frost heave.
deep: An insulated slab with insulated paving prevents freezing under the base and is an alternative to piles.
very_deep: An insulated slab with insulated paving remains an alternative to piles.

1-2: A slab 200 to 300 mm thick is used.
3-5: A thicker slab, up to 400 to 600 mm, is used.
6-10: A slab 400 to 600 mm thick is used.
11-25: Usually built as a combined pile-slab foundation, with the load shared by slab and piles.
26+: A pure slab is rarely used at this height; it is combined with piles.

wood: Minimal load; a thin slab 150 to 200 mm is enough.
aerated_concrete: Aerated concrete combines well with a stiff slab.
brick: High load; a 300 to 400 mm slab with heavier reinforcement is needed.
reinforced_concrete: Maximum load; a slab at least 400 mm thick is needed, often combined with piles.

7: A slab is preferred and needs heavier reinforcement.
8+: One of the better solutions: a monolithic slab moves with the soil and reduces inertial loads on the building.

sand: Best suited when the sand is dry and lies at shallow depth.
sandy_loam: Best suited when the sandy loam is dry and lies at shallow depth.
loam: Usable only when the columns are embedded below the freezing depth.
clay: Frost heave pushes separate columns up unevenly and tilts the building.
fill: Not recommended: unpredictable settlement of the fill supports the columns unevenly.

high: Optimal: each column transfers its load directly to strong soil.
low: Only for very light structures with columns taken down to a dense layer.

high: Main contraindication: buoyancy acts on the columns and embedding them in saturated soil is technically difficult.
medium: Columns must be embedded below the water level and waterproofed.
low: Ideal: columns sit below the freezing depth in dry dense soil.

shallow: Optimal: the required embedment is minimal.
moderate: Columns are embedded about 1.0 to 1.8 m; still cheaper than a strip foundation.
deep: Columns lose their economic advantage; the cost becomes comparable to piles.
very_deep: Not recommended; piles replace column foundations completely.

1-2: The most economical solution for light one-storey buildings; two-storey timber or frame houses need stable soil and low groundwater.
3-5: Categorically not used for 3 storeys and above: separate supports lack stiffness and bearing capacity.
6-10: Categorically not used for 3 storeys and above: separate supports lack stiffness and bearing capacity.
11-25: Categorically not used for 3 storeys and above: separate supports lack stiffness and bearing capacity.
26+: Categorically not used for 3 storeys and above: separate supports lack stiffness and bearing capacity.

wood: Ideal: the minimal load allows small columns.
aerated_concrete: Limited use; a monolithic reinforced concrete grade beam is required because aerated concrete performs poorly in bending.
brick: Not recommended: separate supports do not spread the load of heavy walls evenly.

0-6: Weak influence; columns work without restrictions.
7: Used only to a limited extent, with a mandatory rigid monolithic grade beam.
8+: Not recommended: separate supports risk overturning in an earthquake.

sand: Coarse and medium sand suit a strip well; fine and silty sand loses bearing capacity when saturated.
sandy_loam: Usable when the sandy loam has low moisture content.
loam: Dense loam is an optimal soil for a strip embedded below the freezing depth.
clay: Dense clay suits a strip when groundwater is deep.
fill: The worst soil for a strip: it needs detailed soil analysis, complex construction and high labour input.

high: Optimal: minimal footing width saves concrete.
low: Needs substantial widening or soil replacement under the footing, which hurts the economics.
Ideal: the trench stays dry and the soil keeps its bearing capacity.
medium: Drainage and waterproofing of the strip are needed.
high: Serious limitation: saturated soil loses bearing capacity and deep embedment becomes impractical.

shallow: Optimal: a shallow strip solves the problem.
moderate: The strip is embedded about 1.0 to 1.8 m; still competitive on stable soils with low groundwater.
deep: Embedding 1.8 to 2.3 m makes the strip very expensive; priority shifts to piles.
very_deep: Deepening the strip is economically impractical; the choice shifts to piles.

1-2: A shallow or deep strip is used depending on the soil.
3-5: A deep strip with a wider footing and more reinforcement; 5 storeys only on stable high-capacity soil.
6-10: A pure strip is rarely used above 5 storeys; it is replaced by a slab or piles.
11-25: A pure strip is rarely used above 5 storeys; it is replaced by a slab or piles.
26+: A pure strip is rarely used above 5 storeys; it is replaced by a slab or piles.

wood: Light load; a shallow narrow strip is enough.
aerated_concrete: Aerated concrete needs a rigid base, which a reinforced strip provides.
brick: The classic solution for heavy brick walls, embedded below the freezing depth.
reinforced_concrete: Maximum load; needs a wide deep strip or a switch to a slab.

0-6: Weak influence; a standard strip works without restrictions.
7: A monolithic strip with heavier longitudinal reinforcement is applicable.
8+: Only limited use: the strip must be tied to a slab or grillage to act jointly.
